e-5847.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degrees of the Numerator and Denominator are Equal
e-5847.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{4x^3-x}{3x^3+24}.$
e-5847.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^3.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^3,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{4{x}^{3}-x}{3{x}^{3}+24} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(4-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(3+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ and $\dfrac{24}{x^3}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(4-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(3+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & \to \frac{4-0}{3+0} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y = \dfrac{4}{3}.$

e-5849.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Denominator is Greater
e-5849.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{3x^2+ 2x}{6x^4-1}$.
e-5849.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^4.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^4,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3{x}^{2}+2x}{6{x}^{4}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{6{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(6-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms  $\dfrac{3}{x^2}, \dfrac{2}{x^3},$ and $\dfrac{1}{x^4}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(6-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{6-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y = 0.$

e-5851.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Numerator is Greater

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{2x}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the term $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ becomes very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ≈\frac{2x}{1-0} \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y = f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Denominator is Greater
content.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}+2x-3}{{x}^{3}-x}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+2x-3}{{x}^{3}-x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{1}{x},\frac{2}{{x}^{2}},\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0-0}{1-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{2}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3+4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}-x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+4-2x)}{(1-\frac{1}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+4-2x)}{(1-\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{0+4-2x}{1-0} \\  & =4-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{6-3x+4{x}^{2}}{12x-21} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6}{x}-\frac{3x}{x}+\frac{4{x}^{2}}{x})}{(\frac{12x}{x}-\frac{21}{x})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6}{x}-3+4x)}{(12-\frac{21}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{6}{x}$ and $\frac{21}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{6}{x}-3+4x)}{(12-\frac{21}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{0-3+4x}{12-0} \\  & =\frac{4x-3}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let x→∞.

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is x. So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by x, as follows:

f(x)=6−3x+4x212x−21=(6x−3xx+4x2x)(12xx−21x)=(6x−3+4x)(12−21x)

Now, when x is very large, the terms 6x and 21x become very small. Therefore, as x→∞, we have

f(x)=(6x−3+4x)(12−21x)≈0−3+4x12−0=4x−312.

This is not a constant, which means that y=f(x) does not have a horizontal asymptote.

content.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{6-3x+4{x}^{2}}{12x-21} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6}{x}-\frac{3x}{x}+\frac{4{x}^{2}}{x})}{(\frac{12x}{x}-\frac{21}{x})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6}{x}-3+4x)}{(12-\frac{21}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{6}{x}$ and $\frac{21}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{6}{x}-3+4x)}{(12-\frac{21}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{0-3+4x}{12-0} \\  & =\frac{4x-3}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{x},$ $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{({x}^{2}-\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}})}{(1+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ≈\frac{{x}^{2}-0+0}{1+0} \\  & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.
